In standard node2vec, there is no FFT-based or DCT-based spectral band-pass filter used to remove high-frequency graph noise before random walks. node2vec is a biased random-walk graph embedding method that samples walks using the return parameter p and in-out parameter q, then learns node embeddings with a skip-gram objective. So, if you ask for node2vec’s “FFT filter,” the accurate answer is that such a filter is not part of the original algorithm.

If one were to imagine a hypothetical extension that adds spectral preprocessing, an FFT-based band-pass filter would typically mean transforming a graph signal into the frequency domain, attenuating high-frequency components associated with rapid local variation or noise, and then transforming back before generating walks. In that speculative design, DCT could be used as an alternative real-valued spectral transform, while FFT would be the computational tool for efficient frequency-domain filtering. However, that would be a new hybrid method, not node2vec itself.

So the key point is: node2vec does not define an FFT filter; it uses biased random walks and skip-gram learning instead.
